title: Agent Orchestration Patterns
subtitle: Single-agent loops (ReAct, Plan-and-Execute) and multi-agent coordination (Manager-Worker, Decentralized Handoff).

lessons.title: Structuring Agent Behavior: Agent Orchestration Patterns
lessons.hook: Your agent can perceive, reason, and act — but what happens when a task requires 10 distinct tools or a team of specialists? How does the agent sequence its thinking, avoid deadlocks, and collaborate across workflows?
lessons.bigIdea: Orchestration defines how an agent manages its internal decision-making flow and how multiple agents coordinate across a shared task. In single-agent systems, patterns like Tool Calling Loops, ReAct (Reason + Act), and Plan-and-Execute govern action sequences. When tasks grow complex, multi-agent patterns like Manager-Worker and Decentralized Handoffs distribute responsibility.
lessons.plainEnglish: A solo agent is like a solo freelancer managing their own checklist; multi-agent orchestration is like a project manager delegating specialized tasks to researchers, coders, and editors.
objectives: Contrast single-agent patterns: Tool Calling, ReAct, and Plan-and-Execute
Explain multi-agent coordination models: Manager-Worker and Decentralized Handoffs
Apply decision criteria to choose between single and multi-agent systems
Compare popular orchestration frameworks: LangChain/LangGraph, AutoGen, and CrewAI

sections.title: Single-Agent Orchestration Patterns
sections.content: Even within single-agent systems, decision-making can unfold through different structural patterns:

subsections.title: Tool Calling Loop
subsections.content: The simplest pattern. The model receives a prompt, decides which tool to call, receives output, and repeats until the goal is met or it stops. Best for exploratory searches, but complex tasks can lead to brittle tool chains.

subsections.title: ReAct (Reasoning + Acting)
subsections.content: The model alternates explicit 'Thought' reasoning steps with 'Action' tool calls and 'Observation' steps. Highly transparent and auditable, but increases token usage and latency.

subsections.title: Plan-and-Execute
subsections.content: Separates planning from action. A planner first generates a complete ordered sequence of subtasks, and an execution module carries them out sequentially. Ideal when goals are predictable up front.

sections.title: Multi-Agent Coordination Patterns
sections.content: When tasks span multiple domains, require specialized competencies, or benefit from concurrent parallel execution, multi-agent architectures shine:

subsections.title: Manager-Worker Pattern
subsections.content: A central manager agent decomposes high-level goals into subtasks, delegates them to specialized workers (e.g. Research Worker, Coder Worker), and synthesizes the outputs. Features clear accountability, but the manager is a potential bottleneck and single point of failure.

subsections.title: Decentralized Handoff Pattern
subsections.content: Agents operate as peers without a central boss. Control is passed directly between agents based on task state (e.g., Intake Agent passes to Flight Booking Agent, which triggers Hotel Agent). High autonomy, but requires careful protocols to prevent infinite loops (deadlocks).

sections.title: Choosing the Right Orchestration Strategy
sections.content: Evaluate four key dimensions to determine whether to go solo or deploy a team:

subsections.title: Task Scope and Autonomy Boundaries
subsections.content: Narrow, self-contained tasks fit a single agent. Multi-domain tasks with distinct subgoals benefit from multi-agent isolation.

subsections.title: Specialization of Skills
subsections.content: If a task requires separate domains (e.g. legal compliance, Python coding, customer outreach), specialized agents keep system prompts focused and modular.

subsections.title: Sequential vs. Parallel Execution
subsections.content: Linear tasks run fine on a single agent. Concurrent investigations (e.g. checking competitor prices, analyzing sales data, and reviewing compliance simultaneously) demand multi-agent parallelism.

subsections.title: Observability and Debugging
subsections.content: Single-agent systems centralize logic and are easier to audit. Multi-agent teams require distributed tracing and shared state management.

sections.title: Agent Orchestration Frameworks in Practice
sections.content: Three popular open-source frameworks support these patterns in production:

subsections.title: LangChain & LangGraph
subsections.content: LangGraph structures workflows as executable state graphs with explicit branching logic, human approval cycles, and cyclical retries.

subsections.title: AutoGen (Microsoft)
subsections.content: Centers around dialogue-based multi-agent collaboration, simulating team meetings where agents converse and negotiate.

subsections.title: CrewAI
subsections.content: Built natively around the Manager-Worker model with role-playing crews, shared task queues, and structured delegation.

quiz.question: You are building an AI research assistant that must gather competitor announcements from the web, analyze internal sales reports in parallel, synthesize insights, and obtain human sign-off before publishing. Which orchestration pattern is most appropriate?
options: Manager-Worker multi-agent pattern with parallel worker execution and human approval gate
Decentralized peer handoff with no central coordinator
quiz.correctAnswer: Manager-Worker multi-agent pattern with parallel worker execution and human approval gate
quiz.explanation: Manager-Worker allows parallel subtask delegation (web research + sales analysis), central synthesis by the manager, and clean placement of a human approval gate before final delivery.

quiz.question: What is the primary defining characteristic of the ReAct pattern?
options: It generates all plans in advance and never changes them
It alternates explicit 'Thought' reasoning steps with 'Action' tool calls and 'Observation' feedback steps
It operates exclusively on physical robots
It eliminates the need for large language models
quiz.correctAnswer: It alternates explicit 'Thought' reasoning steps with 'Action' tool calls and 'Observation' feedback steps
quiz.explanation: ReAct stands for Reasoning + Acting, logging explicit thoughts between actions to improve auditability and recovery from unexpected tool outputs.

recap: Single-agent patterns structure internal thinking: Tool Calling (flexible), ReAct (transparent), Plan-and-Execute (structured).
Multi-agent patterns divide labor: Manager-Worker (hierarchical coordination) and Decentralized Handoff (peer-to-peer agility).
Choose multi-agent architectures when tasks benefit from parallel execution, specialized prompt boundaries, or distinct tool permissions.
